name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Matching muscle fibres, actin, and sarcomere

questiontext.text:
Match the following and mark the correct option

Column I Column II
A. Fast muscle fibres i. Myoglobin
B. Slow muscle fibres ii. Lactic acid
C. Actin filament iii. Contractile unit
D. Sarcomere iv. I-band

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Skeletal muscle fibres are classified into red (slow) and white (fast) fibres based on myoglobin content and metabolic pathways. Structurally, myofibrils consist of alternating light (I) and dark (A) bands divided by Z-lines into functional contractile units.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fast muscle fibres have fewer mitochondria and high sarcoplasmic reticulum, relying primarily on anaerobic glycolysis for energy, which leads to lactic acid accumulation. Slow muscle fibres contain abundant myoglobin and mitochondria for sustained aerobic contraction. Actin (thin) filaments are exclusively present in the isotropic light band, known as the I-band. The portion of the myofibril between two successive Z-lines is the sarcomere, which serves as the functional contractile unit of muscle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fast muscle fibres correspond to lactic acid, slow muscle fibres to myoglobin, actin filament to I-band, and sarcomere to contractile unit (A-ii, B-i, C-iv, D-iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Ventral attachment of ribs in humans

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human rib cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs that articulate dorsally with the thoracic vertebrae and, for true ribs, ventrally with the breastbone.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each rib is a thin flat bone connected dorsally to the vertebral column and ventrally to the sternum with the help of hyaline cartilage (for the first seven pairs, called true ribs). The scapula and clavicle form the pectoral girdle, while the ilium is a bone of the pelvic girdle; none of these serve as the attachment site for ribs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ribs are attached ventrally to the sternum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Movable joint between atlas and axis

questiontext.text: What is the type of movable joint present between the atlas and axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synovial joints are freely movable joints characterized by a fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating surfaces and are classified into types such as ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, and saddle joints.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first cervical vertebra (atlas) rotates around the odontoid process of the second cervical vertebra (axis), allowing side-to-side rotational movement of the head. This uniaxial rotational articulation is a pivot joint. In contrast, a saddle joint occurs between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb, a hinge joint occurs at the knee and elbow, and gliding joints occur between carpals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The movable joint present between the atlas and axis is a pivot joint.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Location of ATPase enzyme in muscle

questiontext.text: ATPase of the muscle is located in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Muscle contraction requires energy released from the hydrolysis of ATP during cross-bridge formation between thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each myosin (thick) filament is a polymer of meromyosins. The heavy meromyosin (HMM) component forms a globular head with a short arm projecting outward. This globular head is an active ATPase enzyme and possesses binding sites for both ATP and active sites on actin. Actin, troponin, and actinin are components of thin filaments or Z-lines and do not carry the ATPase activity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ATPase enzyme of the muscle is located in myosin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q05 - Presence of intervertebral disc in vertebrates

questiontext.text: Intervertebral disc is found in the vertebral column of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An intervertebral disc is a fibrocartilaginous cushion located between the centra of adjacent vertebrae, providing flexibility and shock absorption to the vertebral column.

Step 2: Evaluation
Intervertebral discs are a characteristic feature of the mammalian vertebral column, forming cartilaginous joints between adjacent vertebrae. Birds, reptiles, and amphibians lack true intervertebral discs between their vertebrae.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Intervertebral discs are found in the vertebral column of mammals.

questiontext.text: Which one of the following is showing the correct sequential order of vertebrae in the vertebral column of human beings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human vertebral column is organized from the skull downward into five distinct anatomical regions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Moving from the neck (anterior/superior) to the tailbone (posterior/inferior), the vertebral column consists of 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck, followed by 12 thoracic vertebrae in the chest region, 5 lumbar vertebrae in the lower back, 1 fused sacral vertebra in the pelvic region, and 1 fused coccygeal vertebra at the terminal end.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequential order of vertebrae in human beings is Cervical — thoracic — lumbar — sacral — coccygeal.

questiontext.text: Which one of the following pairs is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different types of synovial joints permit specific planes of movement depending on the shape of their articulating surfaces.

Step 2: Evaluation
Between the atlas and axis is a pivot joint; between the carpals are gliding joints; and between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb is a saddle joint. However, the joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the pectoral girdle is a ball and socket joint, allowing multidirectional movement, rather than a hinge joint.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect pair is Hinge joint: between Humerus and Pectoral girdle.

answer.text: Hinge joint: between Humerus and Pectoral girdle
Saddle joint : between carpals and metacarpals of thumb

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q08 - Classification of knee and elbow joints

questiontext.text: Knee joint and elbow joint are examples of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A hinge joint is a synovial joint in which movement is restricted primarily to a single plane (flexion and extension), similar to the hinge of a door.

Step 2: Evaluation
Both the knee joint and the elbow joint permit bending and straightening in one plane only, which is characteristic of a hinge joint. Saddle joints occur in the thumb, ball and socket joints in the shoulder and hip, and pivot joints between the atlas and axis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Knee joint and elbow joint are examples of a hinge joint.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q09 - Movement exhibited by macrophages and leucocytes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cells of the human body exhibit three main types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, and muscular.

Step 2: Evaluation
Specialized immune cells in blood and tissues, such as macrophages and leucocytes, move by forming temporary projections called pseudopodia through the streaming of protoplasm and cytoskeletal microfilaments. This type of movement is called amoeboid movement. Ciliary movement occurs in ciliated epithelia (such as the trachea), and flagellar movement is seen in spermatozoa.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Macrophages and leucocytes exhibit amoeboid movement.

questiontext.text: Which one of the following is not a disorder of bone?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Skeletal disorders affect bones and joints, whereas cardiovascular disorders affect the heart and blood vessels.

Step 2: Evaluation
Arthritis is the inflammation of joints, osteoporosis is an age-related disorder characterized by decreased bone mass and increased fracture risk, and rickets is a bone mineralization disorder caused by vitamin D deficiency. In contrast, atherosclerosis is a disorder of the circulatory system involving the deposition of calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissues in the walls of arteries, making their lumen narrower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Atherosclerosis is not a disorder of bone.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q11 - Identifying incorrect statement about muscle types

questiontext.text: Which one of the following statement is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human muscles are classified into skeletal (striated and voluntary), visceral/smooth (non-striated and involuntary), and cardiac (striated and involuntary) muscles based on location, appearance, and neural control.

Step 2: Evaluation
Heart muscles are cardiac muscles, which are striated and involuntary. Muscles of the hands and legs are skeletal muscles, which are striated and voluntary. Muscles located in the reproductive tracts and the inner walls of hollow visceral organs such as the alimentary canal are smooth (visceral) muscles, which are non-striated (smooth) and involuntary—not striated.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that the muscles located in the inner walls of the alimentary canal are striated and involuntary.

answer.text: The muscles of hands and legs are striated and voluntary
The muscles located in the inner walls of alimentary canal are striated and involuntary
Muscles located in the reproductive tracts are unstriated and involuntary

questiontext.text: Which one of the following statements is true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral and pelvic girdles, which articulate with the forelimbs and hindlimbs, respectively, via socket-like cavities.

Step 2: Evaluation
The pectoral girdle (shoulder girdle) features a depression below the acromion called the glenoid cavity, which articulates with the head of the humerus bone to form the shoulder joint. In contrast, the acetabulum is a cavity in the pelvic girdle that articulates with the head of the femur.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The true statement is that the head of the humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of the pectoral girdle.

answer.text: Head of humerus bone articulates with acetabulum of pectoral girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of pectoral girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with acetabulum of pelvic girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with a glenoid cavity of pelvic girdle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q13 - Striated and involuntary muscles of heart

questiontext.text: Muscles with characteristic striations and involuntary are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cardiac muscle tissue is uniquely specialized to maintain continuous rhythmic contractions throughout life without conscious control.

Step 2: Evaluation
Muscles of the heart (cardiac muscles) display cross-striations like skeletal muscles due to organized sarcomeres, yet their activities are not under the voluntary control of the nervous system (involuntary). Muscles in the wall of the alimentary canal are smooth (non-striated) and involuntary, whereas muscles assisting locomotion and muscles of the eyelids are striated and voluntary.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Muscles that have characteristic striations and are involuntary are the muscles of the heart.

answer.text: Muscles in the wall of alimentary canal

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q14 - Matching sternum, glenoid cavity, and joints

questiontext.text:
Match the followings and mark the correct option

Column I Column II
A. Sternum i. Synovial fluid
B. Glenoid Cavity ii. Vertebrae
C. Freely movable joint iii. Pectoral girdle
D. Cartilaginous joint iv. Flat bones

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human skeletal elements are classified by bone shape, girdle anatomy, and joint mobility.

Step 2: Evaluation
The sternum is a flat bone located on the ventral midline of the thorax. The glenoid cavity is a depression in the scapula of the pectoral girdle that articulates with the humerus. Freely movable (synovial) joints are characterized by the presence of a fluid-filled synovial cavity containing synovial fluid. Cartilaginous joints allow limited movement and are found between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sternum corresponds to flat bones, glenoid cavity to pectoral girdle, freely movable joint to synovial fluid, and cartilaginous joint to vertebrae (A-iv, B-iii, C-i, D-ii).
